title: Blood tests and monitoring
intro: The blood tests and reviews that go with gender-affirming hormone therapy: what is checked for each medicine, when the sample is taken, what it usually aims for, and how to read your results. It is background reading, not a prescription. Fertility, sexual function, PrEP and surgery are on the [Related care and considerations](#/related-care) page. The forms each medicine comes in and the dose ranges are on the [Medicines, doses and formulations](#/doses) page.

body: Blood tests are not something you pass or fail. They tell your prescriber whether the dose is doing what you both want, and whether anything needs watching.

For feminising therapy, Australia's 2026 standards of care recommend keeping trough oestradiol above about 250 pmol/L, without a fixed upper limit, and total testosterone below 2 nmol/L for people who want full suppression [1]. The 2019 position statement suggested 250–600 pmol/L [2].

For masculinising therapy, the usual target is a trough total testosterone of about 10–20 nmol/L, for the long-acting injection, Testogel and cream [1]. Testavan and the short-acting injections are tested at a different time and read against different numbers: see the testosterone sections below [1]. Other guidance: the 2019 position statement and the 2020 Australian GP guides suggest 10–15 nmol/L [2][3][4]; Australia's 2026 standards of care, which this site follows, give about 10–20 [1]. Testosterone also thickens the blood, so haematocrit is checked; at 0.50 L/L (50%) or above, the dose or the interval is usually reviewed [2][3]. The product information for several testosterone injections now also warns about SGLT-2 inhibitors, medicines for diabetes, heart failure or kidney disease such as empagliflozin or dapagliflozin. Taken with testosterone, they have been linked to too many red blood cells, so the blood count is checked more closely [5]. This warning is not yet in every product information, so tell your prescriber if you take one, whatever form of testosterone you use [6].
Reviews cover more than levels: blood pressure, weight, smoking, and how you are going in yourself — mood, energy, sleep, and whether the changes match what you hoped for [2][7].

Screening follows the organs you have, not your gender and not your hormones [2][7]. If you have a cervix, screening is still due every five years, and collecting your own swab is an option that many people find far easier than a speculum examination [8]. The same logic applies to breast or chest tissue, and to prostate tissue, which genital surgery does not remove [7].
list: Feminising — oestradiol and total testosterone; electrolytes and kidney function if you take spironolactone; liver function if you take cyproterone [2][3]
Masculinising — total testosterone, and a full blood count for haematocrit; liver function and lipids as your prescriber decides [2][3]
Either therapy — blood pressure and weight at each review; glucose or HbA1c and lipids periodically, particularly if you have other risk factors [2][7]
Puberty blockers — bone health is monitored, because blockers pause the bone strengthening that puberty normally provides [2][7]

Before starting — baseline bloods (with a pregnancy test if a pregnancy is possible; a routine blood-clotting test is not needed) [19], and a conversation about fertility and about contraception if pregnancy is possible, since neither testosterone nor oestrogen is reliable contraception [2][7]
Sexual health — STI and blood-borne virus testing as relevant to you, the same as for anyone [7]

Timing — Australia's 2026 standards of care suggest a review every three to four months through the first year, then yearly once things are stable [1]. Other guidance: the 2019 position statement suggests three-monthly in the first year, then every six to twelve months [2]. After a change to oestrogen, levels are rechecked six to eight weeks later rather than straight away; after a change to the long-acting testosterone injection, the Equinox guide waits two more injections [3]
sections.note: Screening and monitoring are easy to lose track of when you move between services. Ask your GP to keep a written list of what is due and when, and ask for a copy yourself.

In the first year, you see your doctor about every 3 months.
After that, you go about once a year (some guides say every 6 to 12 months).
If your dose changes, you have a blood test some weeks later. Your doctor tells you when.

body: Each medicine below has its own table: the tests usually done before starting, in the first year, and after that. They are a guide to what to expect, not a schedule to follow on your own. Your prescriber sets the actual timing, and it can change with your health, other medicines and how you are going [1][2].

In the first year, reviews are usually every three to four months [1] (three-monthly in the 2019 position statement [2]). Once things are stable, Australia's 2026 standards of care suggest a yearly review [1]; the position statement suggests every six to twelve months [2]. Each table shows the test, when it is done, what it usually aims for, and when to talk to your prescriber. Under each table, "For clinicians" gives more detail and the page numbers of the sources.
Every review, whatever the medicine, also covers blood pressure, weight, mood and how the changes are going for you [2][7].
sections.note: Each medicine has a blood test guide to print, under its heading. Bring it to your appointment and ask your prescriber to mark which tests apply to you. To keep track of your own results, use the blood test record: [Blood test record](/guides/log-blood-tests.pdf)

Liver deaths have been reported at doses of 100 mg a day and above, mostly in men treated for prostate cancer; Australian guidance for feminising therapy gives 12.5 mg once a week up to 25 mg a day [12][19].

AusPATH lists bicalutamide as not first-line, because of liver and lung harms, including deaths [13]. The lung warning was added to the product information on 9 July 2026 {{SRC:PI-BIC}} and published in the TGA's August 2026 safety update [14].

sections.h: Getting the timing of the blood test right
body: When the sample is taken matters as much as what is measured. Most targets in the guidelines are trough levels — the lowest point, just before the next dose is due [2][3].
A sample drawn at the wrong point can look far too high or too low when nothing is wrong, and lead to a dose change you did not need.

For Testogel or testosterone cream, your prescriber will usually want the sample in the morning before you apply that day's dose [3][1]. For Testavan, it is taken 2 to 4 hours after applying [1]. For the long-acting injection, the test is booked just before the next injection is due rather than soon after one. For the short-acting injections, the sample is usually taken midway between injections [1]. Oestradiol implants are usually tested every 3 months in the first year [10].
sections.note: Ask for the required timing to be written on your pathology form, and tell the collection centre when your last dose was. It takes ten seconds and it saves repeat tests.

body: Lab reports mark results as high or low using the sex on your Medicare or lab record. On hormones, that range may not fit your body. In the first year your prescriber may ask the lab for both the male and the female ranges [1].
A single flagged result is a reason to talk with your prescriber, not to change a dose on your own.

Units: Australian labs report oestradiol in pmol/L, testosterone in nmol/L, and haematocrit as a fraction (0.50 L/L is the same as 50%). Some overseas guidelines and apps use pg/mL and ng/dL instead: 250 pmol/L of oestradiol is about 68 pg/mL, and 10 to 20 nmol/L of testosterone is about 290 to 580 ng/dL. If a number looks very different from the ones on this page, check the unit first (oestradiol pg/mL × 3.671 = pmol/L; testosterone ng/dL × 0.0347 = nmol/L).
sections.listh: Things that can make a result look wrong
list: A sample taken at a different time after the dose from the one your prescriber asked for [1]

Oestradiol gel on the skin where the blood is taken: ask for the sample from the arm you did not put gel on [1]. Doing the same with testosterone gel or cream is a sensible precaution, though the guidelines do not say it
High-dose biotin (in some hair, skin and nail supplements), which can make some oestradiol tests read falsely high: tell the collection centre if you take it [1]
Splitting the dose, or letting tablets dissolve under the tongue, which changes when the level peaks [1]

Haemoglobin and haematocrit: read against the range for your affirmed gender once hormones have had time to work (about 3 months on testosterone, about 6 months on oestradiol). On testosterone, the male range is used [1]
Kidney function (eGFR) is worked out from your creatinine, age and recorded sex, so the change over time tells more than one result [1]
Iron studies: the range for your affirmed gender, unless you are pregnant or have periods (then the female range is used) [1]
